idiom_name: frozen dataclasses Ok/Err plus match/case consumption
implementation_notes: Python's own error channel is the exception, so a Result is hand-written: a frozen dataclass per case - Ok(value) and Err(error) - and a match statement (Python 3.10+) for consumption, which is what libraries such as returns formalize. Dataclasses and structural pattern matching replace the classic class hierarchy, and the whole thing needs no dependency; what it lacks is enforcement, since nothing stops a caller from dropping a bare parse_port(raw) expression - the type annotation Ok[T] | Err[E] plus the pattern match is the contract. Keep the error a code or exception-like value rather than a formatted string, and convert thrown exceptions at the boundary with a decorator-style wrapper so the core stays exception-free.
pitfalls: Nothing enforces consumption: unlike Rust's #[must_use], a bare parse_port(raw) statement is dropped silently; the type checker and review are the enforcement.
Reaching for attributes (result.error) instead of the match bypasses the union discipline and reintroduces access to the wrong case.
Dataclass equality compares payloads, so error values must be value-comparable (an enum or a dataclass), not exception instances.

variants.name: returns Result (library)
variants.implementation_notes: returns implements the contract as a container: Result[Value, Error] with Success(value) and Failure(error), map/bind composition introduced explicitly through railway-oriented programming in its docs, value_or/alt for exits, and structural pattern matching support; ResultE is the alias for exception-style failures. The @safe decorator (future_safe for async) converts a throwing function into one returning Result - the boundary adapter - and the flow/pipe helpers keep chains flat. Choose it where many fallible steps compose and the dependency is acceptable; the hand-rolled dataclass union stays the zero-dependency form.
pitfalls: Static typing needs the library's mypy plugin; without it bind/flow chains degrade to Any and the container stops protecting anything.
@safe catches only the declared exception classes when given a tuple and rethrows everything else, so an unexpected exception still escapes the contract.
Failure stores the exception object, which keeps traceback frames alive; long-lived Result values can pin memory that way.
